stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Marguerite Osei, a civil engineer, attends the opening ceremony for a railway viaduct she designed.

The mayor's speech ran long, the band played twice, and someone pressed a ribbon of ceremonial silk into Osei's hand. She held it without looking at it. When the first freight train eased onto the span, the crowd cheered; Osei did not. She had gone down to the riverbank, where she stood with one palm flat against the nearest stone pier. Through the stone she felt the load arrive, settle, and pass, exactly as she had known it would. Only then did she smile, and only then did she climb back up to the platform, where the applause had already ended.
choices: Although Osei is honored at the opening, the satisfaction she wants comes from feeling the viaduct carry its load as she planned, not from the public celebration.
Although Osei is honored at the opening, she slips away from the crowd because she fears the viaduct may not hold the weight of the first train.
Osei finds the opening ceremony tedious and resents the mayor for delaying the moment when the first train is finally allowed to cross the viaduct.
Osei is so moved by the crowd's cheering for the viaduct that she has to step down to the riverbank to compose herself before returning to the platform.
explanation: Start with the italic introduction: Osei designed the viaduct, and this is its opening. Then follow what she does from start to end. She holds the ceremonial ribbon without looking at it. She does not cheer. She goes down to the pier to feel the train cross, which happens "exactly as she had known it would." She smiles only after that, and by the time she climbs back up, the applause has ended. So her satisfaction comes from feeling the structure perform as she planned, not from the ceremony. Choice A covers the honor, where her attention goes, and why she smiles.

B.why: You correctly saw that Osei separates herself from the celebration, then explained it with the motive that seemed most likely: nerves. The text rules that out. She felt the load pass "exactly as she had known it would," so she had no doubt to resolve. The first half of this choice is right and the second half adds a fear the passage never gives her. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: You noticed that the speech "ran long" and that Osei ignores the ribbon, and you read her detachment as boredom and resentment. The text never says she is annoyed with the mayor or anyone else. Her attention is on the bridge, not against the ceremony. This choice adds a motive the text never gives.

D.why: This reverses the tone. The text says that when the crowd cheered, "Osei did not," and she goes to the riverbank to feel the train cross, not to recover from the cheering. She misses the applause altogether, so it cannot be what moved her.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is an archaeologist excavating the remains of an ancient settlement.

I logged the sherds by depth and grid and hue,
bagged bone and charcoal, numbered every stone,
and wrote the site as something I could know
the way one knows a ledger or a map.
Then, under the lip of a broken jar,
a thumbprint, pressed in clay three thousand years
before my glove: some potter's careless mark.
I set my pencil down. The grid stayed true,
but I could not go back to counting what
I'd measured; someone's hand had measured me.
choices: The speaker describes the careful methods used to record the site, from charting each find's depth to bagging bone and charcoal for later study.
A potter's thumbprint prompts the speaker to abandon the excavation grid, which now seems an inaccurate way to record the settlement's remains.
A potter's thumbprint shifts the speaker from treating the site as data to be logged to sensing the individual person who once lived there.
The speaker regrets a careless moment that left a mark on an ancient jar, realizing that the excavation has damaged what it meant to preserve.
explanation: Restate the poem in plain English. In the first four lines, the speaker records everything methodically and thinks of the site the way one thinks of "a ledger or a map." At "Then," the poem turns: the speaker finds a potter's thumbprint left in the clay three thousand years ago, puts the pencil down, and cannot go back to simply counting, because "someone's hand had measured me." The poem moves from data to a sense of one real person, and Choice C follows that whole movement.

A.why: This describes only the opening lines: the logging, bagging and numbering. It misses the turn at "Then" and the change in the speaker that the rest of the poem is about. It is true, but too narrow.

B.why: You correctly saw that the thumbprint changes the speaker, then guessed that the change is a rejection of the method. The poem says the opposite: "The grid stayed true." What the speaker can't go back to is treating the finds as mere counting, not the grid itself. The first half of this choice is right and the second half contradicts the text.

D.why: This misattributes the word "careless." The "careless mark" belongs to the ancient potter, pressed into the clay three thousand years before the speaker's glove. The speaker damages nothing and expresses no regret. The feeling is closer to awe at another person's presence.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. In the 1950s, Ruth Okafor works as a nurse in a rural vaccination campaign.

By Friday the ledger showed 412 children inoculated, more than any other district on the coast, and Dr. Mensah had written "Excellent" across the bottom in red. Ruth read the word several times on the bus home. Yet the number she kept arriving at was not 412 but one: the boy on the ridge road whose mother had stood in the doorway, arms folded, until Ruth closed her bag. The ledger had no column for him. She found herself wishing it did.
choices: Ruth takes quiet pride in her district's record, which her supervisor has praised as the best result anywhere on the coast.
Ruth worries that Dr. Mensah's praise will be withdrawn once he learns that a mother on the ridge road refused the vaccine.
Although her campaign has been officially praised, Ruth's thoughts keep returning to the one child she was unable to vaccinate.
Ruth is troubled that her ledger leaves out the boy, and she resolves to change how the campaign records families who refuse.
explanation: Follow Ruth from start to finish. The praise comes first, and then 'Yet' turns to what she actually dwells on: 'not 412 but one,' the boy she couldn't reach. Her wish that the ledger had a column for him shows that this one child, not the record, is what stays with her. Only this choice covers both the praise and where her thoughts turn after it.

A.why: You stopped before 'Yet.' The praise and the record are real, but the passage turns away from them. Ruth is not proud. She is preoccupied with the child she missed, so this choice reverses her feeling.

B.why: You gave Ruth a motive the text never mentions. Nothing suggests she is hiding the refusal or fears losing the praise. Her concern is the boy, not her standing with Dr. Mensah.

D.why: This choice gets the first half right, which is why it tempts. She is troubled that the ledger has no place for him. But she only 'found herself wishing' it did. A wish is not a resolution to change the campaign's records, so the second half claims more than the text says.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes a night spent at a backyard telescope.

I logged them as my father taught me:
magnitude, the hour, the patient drift
of Vega past the maple's highest limb.
I kept the columns neat, the pencil sharp.
It was near dawn, the eyepiece cold with dew,
before I looked down at the page and saw
the slant of every figure was his slant,
the night's whole log was in his hand
as much as mine.
choices: The speaker describes the methodical way of recording the brightness and movement of stars that a father once taught.
The speaker comes to see that a night of careful stargazing has also been a way of carrying on a father's practice.
The speaker regrets spending a whole night filling columns with figures instead of simply looking up at the stars.
The speaker comes to see that a father's habits have kept the speaker from developing a way of observing of the speaker's own.
explanation: Restate the poem in plain English. I logged the stars the way my father taught me, and near dawn I saw that my handwriting was his, so the log was as much his as mine. The turn at 'before I looked down' is a recognition: the speaker's careful observing carries the father's practice forward. Nothing in the poem says this is a loss.

A.why: You summarized the opening lines and skipped the turn. The poem's point is what the speaker realizes near dawn, not the method of logging.

C.why: You added a regret the poem doesn't contain. The speaker keeps the columns 'neat' and 'sharp' with no sign of wishing the night had gone differently, and the ending is a discovery, not a complaint.

D.why: You caught the turn toward the father and then gave it the wrong meaning. Seeing his hand in the log is not presented as a limitation. Nothing says the speaker has been held back from an independent style.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a memoir. As a teenager, the narrator joined a volunteer bird survey on a coastal marsh.

I had come for herons, or at least an osprey, and by the third morning I had counted nothing but sparrows: brown, quick, maddeningly alike. Mr. Haskell, who ran the survey, handed me his own field guide without comment. I began to notice the streaked breast of one, the yellow fleck above the eye of another, the way a third flicked its tail twice before it flew. By the end of the week I had stopped looking up at the sky at all.
choices: Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator gradually becomes absorbed in the differences among the common ones.
Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator grows too discouraged by the week's end to keep scanning the sky.
With the help of Mr. Haskell's field guide, the narrator learns to identify several species of sparrow found on a coastal marsh.
Resenting Mr. Haskell for assigning a newcomer to sparrows, the narrator spends the week counting birds without much interest.
explanation: Trace the emotion. It starts as frustration ('maddeningly alike') and moves into close, specific noticing: the streaked breast, the yellow fleck, the double tail flick. The final line confirms the change. The narrator stopped looking up for herons because the sparrows below had become absorbing.

B.why: You read the last sentence literally and stopped there. The narrator did stop looking at the sky, but out of absorption, not discouragement. The sentences right before it show growing attention, which reverses the tone this choice gives.

C.why: This is roughly true but too narrow. It names what the narrator learned and leaves out the change in feeling from disappointment to absorption, which is what the passage is about.

D.why: You invented a grievance. Mr. Haskell only hands over a field guide, and the narrator's interest grows. It doesn't stay low.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Archaeologist Lena Varga has spent eleven seasons searching for a ruler's tomb.

The trench opened not onto a burial chamber but onto a kitchen: a hearth ringed with soot, three cracked storage jars, a grinding stone worn into a shallow bowl. Her students were careful with her that evening, speaking softly, as one does around a loss. Lena let them. She did not explain that she had spent the afternoon with her palm pressed to the hollow of that stone, fitting her hand to the shape another hand had made, and that she had not wanted a king for hours.
choices: Although Lena hides her disappointment from her students, failing to find the tomb after eleven seasons weighs heavily on her.
Although Lena is moved by the find, she hides this from her students because she fears they will think her long search was wasted.
Although the trench held no tomb, it revealed a hearth, storage jars, and a grinding stone used by the valley's ordinary residents.
Although her students assume the find is a disappointment, Lena is deeply absorbed by the traces of ordinary life it reveals.
explanation: The students treat the evening 'as one does around a loss,' but the last sentence shows what Lena actually felt. She spent the afternoon fitting her hand to the worn stone and 'had not wanted a king for hours.' The passage turns on the gap between what the others assume and what she feels.

A.why: You took the students' view as Lena's. The final sentence shows she isn't grieving at all, so this reverses her feeling.

B.why: The first half is right. She is moved, and she doesn't tell her students. But the text never says why she stays silent. The fear that her search will look wasted is a motive you supplied.

C.why: This lists what the trench contained and leaves Lena out entirely. A literary main idea has to cover the character's response, and that response is the point of the passage.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Tomasz's textile mill has just stopped paying workers by the piece and begun paying them by the hour.

The new wage was, by the foreman's arithmetic and his own, eleven cents an hour more than he had ever averaged at the old rate. Yet on the first Monday Tomasz caught himself glancing at the tally board where his count used to climb in chalk, and finding it wiped clean, he worked the loom more slowly than he meant to, as if something had been taken from the hour along with the counting.
choices: Though Tomasz earns more under the new system, he misses the higher pay he could reach on his fastest days at the old rate.
Though Tomasz earns more under the new system, he senses that something has gone out of his work now that it is no longer counted.
Though Tomasz welcomes the raise, he deliberately slows his work at the loom to protest the mill's decision to stop counting.
Tomasz checks the foreman's arithmetic and confirms that the new hourly wage is higher than his average at the old piece rate.
explanation: The first sentence settles the money question: he is better paid. 'Yet' turns to what actually affects him, which is the blank tally board, the slower work, and the sense that 'something had been taken from the hour along with the counting.' What he has lost is the count, not pay.

A.why: You saw that Tomasz feels a loss and assumed it must be money. The passage never mentions peak earnings. What is taken 'along with the counting' is not income.

C.why: He works more slowly 'than he meant to,' so the slowdown is not deliberate. A protest is a motive the text rules out.

D.why: This is true, but it covers only the first sentence. It ignores the 'Yet' and the feeling that follows, and that feeling is the main idea.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker works in a laboratory that measures the nutrients in food.

All week I weigh the lentils into grams,
burn them to ash, and read what's left: the iron,
the zinc, a little magnesium, the sum
of what a body takes from what it eats.
My mother never weighed a thing. She fed us
by the fistful and the look on our faces.
And only on the Friday drive back home
did I think she had been measuring as well,
just not in any unit I was taught.
choices: The speaker describes the laboratory process of reducing lentils to ash in order to measure the minerals they contain.
The speaker regrets that a mother who never weighed food could not give her children the nutrients a laboratory would advise.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as its own kind of careful measurement.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as more accurate than the laboratory's methods.
explanation: In plain English: at work I measure food precisely, my mother never measured anything, and on the drive home I realized she had been measuring too, just in units I wasn't taught. The 'only then' turn reframes the mother's feeding by eye as another form of measurement.

A.why: You described the first stanza's images and missed the turn. The lab work sets up the reflection about the mother and isn't the poem's point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The speaker ends by crediting the mother ('measuring as well'), not by faulting her diet.

D.why: This gets the realization right and then ranks it. The poem calls her measuring different ('not in any unit I was taught'), not better. 'More accurate' is a comparison the speaker never makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Decades ago, Arturo Llosa was chief engineer on a bridge that his granddaughter is now driving him across.

Inés wanted him to be proud, and slowed on the center span so he could look. He did not look at the river. He was listening for the expansion joints, the double knock of each tire passing over, and for the faint drag that would mean a bearing had begun to seize. There was none. He let out a breath he would not have admitted holding, and only then, with the far bank in view, did he tell her it was a good bridge.
choices: Arturo cannot share his granddaughter's simple pride in the bridge until he has privately satisfied himself that it is still sound.
Arturo is indifferent to his granddaughter's pride in the bridge, having long since stopped caring about his earlier work.
Arturo hears a bearing beginning to seize as they cross, and he keeps this from his granddaughter so as not to spoil her pride.
Arturo shows his granddaughter how the bridge's expansion joints and bearings have kept it sound over many decades.
explanation: Inés wants him to admire the bridge, but he listens anxiously for faults instead. After 'There was none' and the breath he was holding, 'only then' does he praise it. The last sentence brings it together: his approval comes only after he has quietly checked that the bridge is sound.

B.why: Listening closely and holding his breath are signs of intense concern. This choice reverses that into not caring.

C.why: You noticed his anxiety and his concealment ('would not have admitted') and finished the thought the obvious way. But the text says 'There was none.' He finds no fault, so there is nothing to hide.

D.why: Arturo never explains anything to Inés. The joints and bearings are what he listens to in silence, and the passage is about his private worry, not a lesson in engineering.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. In 1931, Hester Crane is mapping a river valley that a new reservoir will soon flood.

The commission wanted contours and property lines, nothing more; the valley would be water by spring. Hester gave them those. But she also marked the ford where the cattle crossed, the orchard wall, and the name the Pruitt children used for the hill behind their school, which appeared in no deed. Her supervisor struck these from the final sheet as unnecessary. She kept her field copy, folded small, in the drawer where other people keep letters.
choices: Hester records the valley's daily life beyond her official task, hoping the fuller map will persuade the commission not to flood it.
Hester resents the commission for flooding the valley and keeps her field copy as proof that the official map is inaccurate.
Hester gives the commission the contours and property lines it requires for a valley that will be under water by spring.
Hester records the valley's daily life beyond her official task and treasures that record even after it is cut from the map.
explanation: 'But she also marked' shows Hester going past the assignment to record the ford, the wall and the children's name for the hill. After those details are struck, she keeps her copy 'in the drawer where other people keep letters,' which tells you she treasures it as something personal. Only this choice covers both her going beyond the task and how she treats the result.

A.why: The first half is exactly right, which is why it tempts. But the flood is settled ('would be water by spring'), and nothing says she hopes to stop it. The persuasion motive is your addition.

B.why: The text shows no resentment and never calls the official map inaccurate. It is only missing details. Keeping the copy among 'letters' points to attachment, not to gathering evidence.

C.why: This is true but covers only the first two sentences. It skips everything after 'But,' which is where the passage's real interest lies.
